transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-31 16:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sophie Chen (HelixWare Head of ML), Daniel Park (HelixWare Platform Eng), Rita Gomez (HelixWare CTO)

Auto-summary: quick discovery; HelixWare is evaluating an inference partner for a multilingual agent product; heavy emphasis on context length (8k->32k), tool-calling for internal connectors, and strong compliance (on-prem & VPC).

[00:00] Aisha: all right hi everyone thanks for taking the time, i'm aisha from Redwood, should we do quick intros?
[00:08] Sophie: yeah hi i'm sophie, head of ml at helixware, we run the conversational assistant product.
[00:12] Daniel: daniel here platform, i'll be owning infra side.
[00:15] Rita: rita, cto, brief here but i'll jump in re: compliance questions.
[00:20] Marco: marco ruiz, se on inference and deployment, happy to dig into latencies and runtime.

[00:35] Aisha: cool, quick agenda: understand your stack and goals, talk model choices (open models), context & multilingual needs, and then deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private). also we'll capture next steps. sound good?
[00:45] Sophie: yup, especially interested in how open models behave for long documents and for french/spanish.

[02:10] Marco: can you walk me through typical call patterns and sequence lengths? like are you doing single-shot or long-context summarizations?
[02:22] Sophie: mostly long context, we have multi-turn customer threads, attachments, sometimes full chat histories up to about 18k tokens, ideally support to 32k. sometimes we do tool-calling to query internal DBs or inject vector-search results.
[02:38] Marco: okay that's helpful. one nuance is that many open models have different kv cache behavior; our runtime can stream and manage KV cache so the effective perf for 20-32k depends on kernel selection and quantization.

[03:50] Daniel: curious re: hosted, if we go hosted where does data land? we have residency requirements for EU customers.
[03:58] Aisha: in hosted we keep data in region you select; for EU traffic we use EU regions and we have retention controls, but for strict regulatory folks we recommend dedicated or private.

[05:10] Rita: SOC2 and SSO — do you support SAML2? we need KMS integration for key wrapping.
[05:18] Marco: yes we support SAML / OIDC, RBAC on the console, and KMS/HSM integrations for private deployments. hosted has customer-scoped keys for encryption at rest and in transit; private gives you full control.

[06:30] Sophie: on models, we tried llama-variants and some of the instruction-tuned ones; cost is a big driver but so is quality on non-english. any guidance on model families for multilingual and long context?
[06:45] Marco: yes. rough guidance: larger decoder-only open models with context-aware optimizations perform better for long context, but there are tradeoffs: quantized 4-bit variants save cost but can slightly degrade certain languages. for multilingual, finetuned or family models with explicit multilingual pretraining (x-glm, mPT derivatives) tend to be stronger. we can run side-by-side evals — that's what we normally recommend.

[08:05] Sophie: can you give an example of latency vs cost for say 8k vs 32k?
[08:12] Marco: high level: for a 1k token generation at 8k context you might see p99 latency ~120-180ms on a dedicated 80GB GPU for optimized kernels; at 32k the KV walk and memory pressure can push that to 300-600ms unless you use chunked retrieval and smarter caching. hosted may add network tail but we have routing to minimize that. cost per token increases because of longer attention windows and kv memory — batching helps but needs workload patterns.

[10:00] Daniel: we definitely don't want 500ms p99 for user-facing chat; our target is p99 < 250ms for 90% of interactions. is that realistic?
[10:12] Marco: yes for most scenarios with 8k context and a trimmed model you can hit that on dedicated. for 32k it's tight; options: use a shorter context window for the model at runtime, prefix KV caching to pre-embed long history, or route heavy-context requests to lower-latency dedicated pools.

[11:50] Sophie: tool-calling — we need robust function-calling to hit internal endpoints and to enforce schema. do open models support that?
[12:00] Marco: we support tool-calling at the API layer; model support is a mix — some instruction-tuned open models can do structured output, others need prompt engineering. Redwood's function-calling shim lets you define contract schemas and enforces safety checks; for private you can run transformers that are instruction-tuned with function-call supervision.

[14:10] Rita: how do you handle fallbacks if a model fails or latency spikes? we have SLAs.
[14:20] Aisha: we have smart routing and automatic fallback policies — route to a smaller/cheaper model or a regional replica. Dedicated customers can define canary and A/B rollouts plus automatic fallback to a hosted variant if capacity is constrained.

[15:45] Sophie: was curious about quantization specifics, marco you mentioned 4-bit — does that affect multilingual nuance?
[15:55] Marco: depends on the quantization recipe. some 4-bit q8_q4 and group-wise quant methods preserve the softer tokens. we run evals on your prompt set to measure BLEU/chrF for non-English. small regressions for rare language idioms can happen but often acceptable for many production flows.

[18:00] Daniel: network and VPC: if we select private, is it an on-prem bundle or VPC peering? and what's the onboarding time?
[18:10] Marco: both. Private supports VPC peering for cloud-hosted private control plane and also an on-prem appliance for air-gapped setups. onboarding time: VPC deployment ~2-4 weeks (depends on approvals), on-prem is longer and we do a joint project plan.

[20:05] Sophie: bench strategy — recommend we run identical prompts on hosted, dedicated reserved pool, and private with a smaller q4 model?
[20:14] Marco: yes, we'll run identical benchmark harness with your prompts and measure latency, p95/p99, cost/token, and quality metrics (ROUGE/BLEU/semantic-similarity). we'll also test tool-calling success rate and structured output accuracy.

[22:40] Rita: compliance docs — can you send SOC2 report and data flow diagrams?
[22:45] Aisha: yes we'll share our security pack and a redacted SOC2; for deeper audit we can set up a security meeting.

[24:30] Sophie: how do you recommend splitting routing between hosted and dedicated for cost control? like hybrid routing?
[24:40] Marco: common pattern: route low-sensitivity, low-latency traffic to hosted for cost efficiency; route high-sensitivity or high-throughput endpoints to dedicated. we can also use dynamic routing by cost threshold or latency SLOs — Redwood Optimize suggests batching and cache settings by route.

[26:55] Daniel: what about model updates and rollouts, we need version pinning.
[27:03] Marco: you can pin model versions at route level, roll out canary traffic percentage, automatic rollback on quality regressions. we also keep detailed token-level cost and trace for debugging.

[29:20] Sophie: any gotchas with embeddings / vector store integration? we use faiss.
[29:28] Marco: embeddings: we offer batch/streaming endpoints and you can run your own vector store; we support connector patterns to push embeddings to Faiss, Pinecone, or your internal store. watch out for normalization differences; we'll help with best practices.

[31:10] Rita: what's the commercial model for dedicated — reserved capacity vs bursts?
[31:18] Aisha: dedicated has monthly/annual commits; you can configure burst capacity for seasonal spikes. pricing is combination of reserved instance fee + usage. we'll provide a matrix in the follow-up.

[33:40] Sophie: do you have any public benchmarks for non-English?
[33:45] Marco: we have internal multilingual evals, and we can run a bespoke eval on your prompts. public benchmarks vary by model family but we'll share our baseline reports.

[35:00] Daniel: what's the minimum pilot size? we can start with a 2-week pilot on hosted then expand to dedicated if numbers look good.
[35:08] Aisha: that works. typical pilot is 2-4 weeks for benching + integration. we can scope an initial POC that includes one route, tooling for function calls, and automated evals.

[37:30] Sophie: question on observability — can we see token-level tracing and per-route cost?
[37:36] Marco: yes console gives token-level breakdowns, traces, and error logs. for private we can send logs to your SIEM.

[39:50] Rita: any competitor differences we should be aware of? like other vendors that claim lower latency — how is redwood different?

[40:00] Marco: a lot of competitors focus on API simplicity; our difference is runtime optimizations (kernels, kv cache management), unified control plane across hosted/dedicated/private, and cost-aware controls. we'll show specifics in the follow-up.

[42:20] Sophie: okay want to recap next steps?
[42:25] Aisha: recap — we will: 1) share pricing & cost/latency matrix, 2) run benchmark with your 100 prompts across hosted/dedicated/private quantized variants, 3) send security pack and SOC2, 4) schedule infra deep-dive.
[42:45] Daniel: agreed, i'll send prompts and a quick traffic profile.
[42:50] Rita: i'll connect legal/security contacts after i confirm list.

[44:00] Aisha: perfect, i'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep-dive and the benchmark kickoff. any final Qs?
[44:08] Sophie: none from me, thanks.
[44:12] Marco: thanks everyone, looking forward to the bench.
[44:18] Rita: thank you.

[47:30] End of recording

Notes: minor transcription artifacts: 'K-V cash' instead of KV cache, some product names transcribed imperfectly. The team emphasized evaluation on multilingual metrics and structured tool-calls; pilot agreed for 2 weeks with benchmarks.
